title: CMAs with Craig - June 17, 2026
summary: Craig walks through two live CMA analyses: a 1950s off-market bungalow in Rose Park (Salt Lake City) needing TLC, and a 1925 outdated home on 4.74 acres in Highland with subdivision potential. Covers comp selection, condition adjustments, acreage valuation, investor flip math, seller financing exclusions, and highest-and-best-use analysis for land subdivision.

broker_guidance.guidance: Start with tax records and a map view to get an outside visual. Check county parcel detail for square footage, finished basement percentage, and acreage. Never assume basement finish from total sqft alone—verify above-grade vs below-grade separately.
broker_guidance.client_language: Let me pull the tax records and county parcel details first to verify square footage, finished area, and lot size before we run comps.

broker_guidance.guidance: Narrow geography first—stay within natural boundaries (rivers, highways) and avoid crossing major dividers like I-15. Then filter by property type (bungalow/rambler), year built range, and square footage bracket. If too many comps, tighten criteria; if too few, expand days back or relax filters. Software typically sorts higher sales to the right—focus on the lower side for fixer properties.
broker_guidance.client_language: We’re keeping comps within Rose Park, same era, similar size. The higher-priced sales on the right are remodeled—those don’t apply to your property.

broker_guidance.scenario: Property needs significant TLC / not updated
broker_guidance.guidance: When no hammered comps exist in recent sales, expand days back (e.g., 180 or 270 days) and exclude price points you know are too high. Walk each comp’s photos and estimate a dollar discount versus the subject. If the best available comp is still $30–50K nicer, apply that discount mentally and document it.
broker_guidance.client_language: Even the roughest recent comp is still $30–40K nicer than what we’re walking into, so we need to discount further. I’m expanding the search to 270 days to find more realistic comparables.

broker_guidance.scenario: Seller is looking at Zillow or public sites for pricing
broker_guidance.guidance: Explain that Zillow shows after-repair values, not as-is condition. Neighbor’s house sold for $450K after it got fixed up—not before. Investors will calculate 70% of ARV minus repairs, which is typically far below owner-occupant market value.
broker_guidance.client_language: Your neighbor’s house sold for $450K after it was renovated. Investors will offer around 70% of that minus repair costs. Listing to an owner-occupant buyer will net you more.

broker_guidance.scenario: Investor flip offer vs listing to owner-occupant
broker_guidance.guidance: If the home is habitable, an owner-occupant buyer will almost always pay more than an investor flipper who needs profit margin. For flip math: find remodeled comps, estimate remodel cost, add flipper profit, and work backward. But if habitable, list to retail buyers first.
broker_guidance.client_language: If the home is livable, we should list it retail. An owner-occupant will outbid an investor who needs to build in profit and renovation costs.

broker_guidance.scenario: Large acreage property with subdivision potential
broker_guidance.guidance: Verify zoning with the city—some areas use density (number of homes) rather than minimum lot size. Calculate value two ways: (1) keep the home on a smaller retained lot and sell off subdivided parcels, or (2) knock down and sell as bare lots. Engage an architect or engineer to map out possible lot configuration. Compare total subdivided value against as-is single-sale value.
broker_guidance.client_language: Before we price this, we need to know how many lots the city will allow. If it’s five lots by density, five smaller lots may be worth more than one big parcel—even though each individual lot drops in value.

broker_guidance.guidance: When acreage is a determining factor, filter comps by lot size first. If comps have varying lot sizes, assign a per-square-foot or per-acre value and adjust accordingly. Be cautious with outliers—comps with far more acreage can skew the analysis and may need to be discounted or removed.
broker_guidance.client_language: Acreage is critical here, so I’m filtering comps by lot size and will adjust for any differences. That outlier with excessive acreage is going to be discounted because it’s not comparable.

broker_guidance.scenario: Seller wants to sell to a flipper instead of listing
broker_guidance.guidance: Set expectations early: flippers need profit margin. They’ll take 70% of after-repair value and subtract repairs. If the seller’s expectation is based on fixed-up neighbor sales, they need to understand the difference between as-is and ARV pricing.
broker_guidance.client_language: If you sell to a flipper, expect an offer around 70% of the fixed-up value minus renovation costs. If you want top dollar, we list it as-is to a retail buyer.

steps: Pull tax records and county parcel details for verified square footage, finished basement, and acreage
View the property on a map to understand boundaries and neighborhood context
Set initial comp filters: geography, property type, year built, square footage
If too many comps, tighten criteria; if too few, expand days back or relax filters
Review comp photos and condition to estimate dollar adjustments for the subject property
Exclude remodeled/high-end comps for fixer properties; focus on the lower end of the price spectrum
For properties needing TLC, expand search to 180–270 days if needed and exclude price points that don’t apply
Explain to sellers that Zillow and public sites show after-repair values, not as-is pricing
For acreage properties, verify zoning rules (density vs lot size) before pricing
Calculate subdivision potential by comparing total value of split lots vs single as-is sale
If habitable, recommend listing to owner-occupant buyers rather than selling to investors
Create a CMA packet with selected comps and email PDF to the agent

objections.objection: Seller says their neighbor sold for much more
objections.response: That neighbor sale was after renovation. Your home is as-is. Investors will offer 70% of ARV minus repairs. Listing retail to an owner-occupant gets you closer to market value.

objections.objection: Seller wants to sell to a flipper to avoid hassle
objections.response: Flippers need margin. They’ll start at 70% of fixed-up value and deduct repairs. You’ll net significantly less than listing as-is to a buyer who will live in it.

objections.objection: Seller thinks Zillow estimate is accurate
objections.response: Zillow reflects after-repair values of updated homes nearby, not the as-is condition of your property. Our CMA uses actual comparable sales matched to your home’s current condition.

objections.objection: Large acreage—seller wants one price for the whole parcel
objections.response: We need to check zoning first. If density allows five lots, five smaller lots may total more than one big parcel. Let’s get an engineer to map it before we set a price.
